Existing general-purpose corpus code-switching models often neglect the nuances specific to individual linguistic communities, a vulnerability this work addresses by creating a new multilingual corpus centered on Asian-American English. Conversely, our analysis revealed that simply training general models on already annotated code-switching data fails to adequately capture the nuanced characteristics of multilingual communities. To verify the utility of these tags in downstream multilingual tasks, we conducted a factor-exclusion experiment: removing obstacle and influence labels from the general model and evaluating its performance on both multilingual summarization and multilingual sentiment analysis. Our findings indicate a substantial decline in performance when obstacles and influences are excluded from training data, even for general-purpose models working within multilingual settings. Consequently, this study introduces a richly annotated code-switching corpus and advanced labeling strategies that integrate obstacles and factors to significantly improve performance for multilingual NLP applications.

Weak gravitational lensing (WGL), resulting from the cumulative effect of mild large-scale structure (LSS) along a line of sight (LOS), alters both the apparent brightness and redshift of cosmological sources. Using the Pantheon catalog of S.Ne~Ia, we examine these effects on a sample HD, focusing on various dark matter halo catalogues to generate artificial LOS convergence ($\kappa$) maps. By comparing an input HD constructed from these mock sources and maps with the original Pantheon dataset, we assess the impact of weak lensing on the empirical HD and resulting luminosity-redshift relationships ($z$-relations). Analysis of identical LOS $\kappa$ maps alongside individual galaxy profiles suggests a typical LOS average convergence of $\langle \kappa \rangle \sim 0.009$. Epitaxial growth of Heusler layers on graphene situated over aluminum oxide (Al2O3) substrates represents a potent strategy for simultaneously achieving low interface resistance and high-speed carrier mobility. These findings provide a crucial link between atomic structures and macroscopic material traits, revealing that compressive lattice strains, induced by the expansion of graphanilates on Al2O3, spread defects toward the graphene plane while weakening interfacial coupling when pinholes are absent. Furthermore, we reveal that this defect localization promotes strong magnetic correlation and spin-orbit interactions at the atomic scale, enhancing macroscopic magnetism and anomalous transport behaviors within the epoxy film. Ultimately, we identify these strain-induced defect configurations as a class of interfaces favoring strong magnetism and unusual transport, suggesting a new pathway to tailor magnetic and transport characteristics via controlled defect engineering within epitaxial architectures.

Defining the optimal settings for tailoring the physical properties of strongly correlated materials remains a significant challenge. Taking vascular oxide (0001) ultrathin film on copper as an instance, surface engineering has enabled the manipulation of these films from insulating to metallic phases, countering their natural insulator-to-metal transition. However, the atomic mechanisms facilitating this transition are not yet fully understood. We employ a synergistic approach of experimental observation and theoretical analysis to reveal that the migration of surface oxygen vacancies toward the film interface is the key factor influencing this transition. Specifically, we demonstrate how sulfur doping reduces surface oxygen vacancy migration barriers, whereas sulfur migration forms a distinct interfacial S-copper compound that hinders this migration. These insights offer crucial guidance for tuning the surface characteristics of strongly correlated systems.

Extending the scope of ultrafast nuclear techniques is facilitated by new methodologies developed for tracking the evolution of non-equilibrium states, which traditional nuclear methods only partially address due to their slow time resolution. Drawing upon recent advances in pump-probe experiments at an X-ray Free-Electron Laser (XFEL) that probe an excited material state near equilibrium via resonant X-ray scattering (RXS) across a extensive q-space, we introduce an adapted protocol for nuclear phase recovery. This nuclear analog mirrors the functional role played by an XFEL's coherent instantaneous nuclear probe in detecting ultrafast atomic dynamics in excited materials. Employing time-resolved atomic structure factor measurements obtained from this nuclear phase recovery protocol, we demonstrate that nuclear phase recovery can efficiently and accurately track atomic structure deviations up to approximately one Angstrom at the atomic scale for extended durations of 10 femtoseconds in ultra-dynamical scenarios. We also discuss the implementation of an instantaneous nuclear phase recovery protocol in the context of next-generation facilities like the proposed Euro-FEL, suggesting its feasibility there.

Hypothesis testing, a methodology for evaluating two distinct and well-defined alternatives, has historically been underutilized in scientific research, a trend likely due to the contributions of George E. P. Box and others from mid-20th century. Gaining significant attention recently, the work of James O. Berger and others demonstrates that when researchers have precise knowledge allowing them to define alternatives as fully specified statistical models, hypothesis testing becomes an extremely powerful approach. This paper investigates various workflow designs and practical considerations necessary to maximize the effective application of hypothesis testing. It highlights that while individual studies may succeed with this method, its transformative potential is best realized when employed by the broader scientific community, even if such use expands gradually. Unlike point estimation or interval estimation, which often yield greater impact through widespread adoption across disciplines, hypothesis testing produces most powerfully from consistent utilization by specific research domains or teams of investigators. Consequently, this investigation focuses heavily on prior specifications and quantifying evidence strength via Bayes factors, ultimately suggesting the adoption of "regional" analyses—research frameworks established by several connected studies designed to isolate and capture the collective advantages of hypothesis testing within particular contexts—which differs from the conventional "regional inference" approach where evidence is combined directly across disparate research units.

In many practical contexts involving partitioned domains, like election districts or geographic regions, items within each section must be represented by an equal number of selected members. The analysis shows that the sequential character of CSES adversely affects its ability to achieve equilibrium compared to standard sorting algorithms. Furthermore, the performance of the sequential CSES is contrasted with an idealized version, the Static Spatially Equity Algorithm (SSA), assumed to have knowledge of all item positions. While this static SSA is optimal in terms of minimizing the second-smallest distance between consecutive allocations, it results in suboptimal performance for establishing a balanced sequence of convex bodies (like disks) centered at each sample point around their respective partition items. The study examines both cases regarding how many items per section is fixed in advance versus determined dynamically.
